eingabe.text:
In this town, when you turn eighteen, you hide until sunrise, or it finds you. We call it Mister Hundred. It's tall enough to look in upstairs windows, and it keeps both hands over its face. It never peeks. At midnight, it counts to one hundred, slow and deep, and the whole town hears it. Your breath turns white when it's close. When it finds you, it bends down and takes its hands away from its face. In the morning, all that's left are your shoes, side by side.

The town calls it Hiding Night. There's only one rule. Nobody can help you hide. If they try, it takes them too. You can't run, either.

On his eighteenth birthday, Owen Pike drove all night. At sunrise, his truck was back in front of his house, engine running. His shoes were on the seat, side by side.

Nobody here plays hide and seek, not even for fun. Nobody leaves their shoes side by side. And nobody ever says the word "ready." That's what it asks when it's done counting.

On Friday, I turned eighteen. My sister June is the only one who ever made it to sunrise. Six years ago, Dad hid her in the crawl space under her room. In the morning, she climbed out. Dad's shoes were on the porch. Every night since, June counts to one hundred before she falls asleep. She says it helps. At breakfast, she took my hand.

[softly] "It never looks in my room, Rabbit." "I'll hide you there." "I promise."

[nervous] At sunset, I went upstairs to grab a flashlight. My breath turned white. Mister Hundred was standing in our yard, six hours early. It wasn't counting. It was looking at me, through its fingers.
